March was for short stories selected by members, and April was The Overstory. The January and February titles already had reading notes on the site, while the other two pages were marked as waiting for notes from the discussion leaders. Mina said she had kept the book titles in the same order as the printed handout so people would not have to compare two different lists. The location stayed the same for all four dates.

A second part of the page explained the accessibility work. The club had paid a freelance captioning and transcript service to prepare captions for three short recordings from the autumn author talks. The audio files were already on the club site, but the captions had not been added to the recordings before this work. The service also supplied plain text transcripts, which Mina linked below each recording rather than putting them into one long document. The actual charge recorded for the three recordings and transcripts was $120.21, not $72.94. The first amount appeared on the receipt in the treasurer’s folder, while $72.94 had been typed into the draft notice by mistake.

His note in the shared document read, “120.21 not 72.94,” and Mina changed the draft to match the receipt. The two amounts referred to the same captioning and transcript service, not to separate charges. The club had not paid another fee for the website that month. Jonas also asked that the notice say the captions were available on the three autumn recordings, rather than suggesting the club had added captions to every recording on its site. Mina adjusted that sentence but left the rest of the page in place.

A regular member, Ruth Bell, said, “I usually open the schedule on the bus, so having the dates near the top helps.” Another member, David Kim, asked whether the reading notes would stay available after the winter schedule ended. Mina replied that the existing notes would remain where they were, and that the two new notes would be added after their discussion leaders sent them. She did not promise a date for those notes. The web volunteer also kept the text size and link colors consistent with the other club pages.

Before sending the link, Jonas compared the amount on the published notice with the receipt, and Mina checked that each recording opened from the page. The club secretary, Elena Ruiz, read through the meeting dates against the printed handout. They found that the April date was shown as the second Thursday, as were the other three dates. The date list included the year, 2026, and the page displayed the time zone used by the library’s local calendar. The committee did not change the location or the book choices during this review.

It did not list anyone’s personal phone number. The club’s general email address was already printed in the website footer, so Mina did not repeat it in the notice. The captioning service’s name was included under the three transcript links, and the charge was described as the cost for that work. The receipt stayed in Jonas’s records and was not uploaded to the public page.

On Friday morning, Mina sent the corrected page link to the committee’s mailing list, and Elena forwarded it to the members. The mailing mentioned that the winter schedule was online and that the autumn recordings now had captions and transcripts. It did not repeat the discussion of the incorrect draft amount. The first meeting remained set for the second Thursday in January at 6:30 p.m. in the Alder Street branch library’s back room. The page continued to show the later dates, reading selections, archive link, transcript links, and the contact line in their separate sections.

last saturday the harbor shelf reading club opened a new version of its website, after several months of planning and small tests. the site went live at 10 a.m., while the club's regular meeting was beginning in the back room of the north pier library. members could use the old site earlier that morning, but the new pages appeared when they refreshed. no public launch event was held, and the club did not change its meeting schedule for the release. the update was meant to make the reading list and meeting details easier to find, especially for people who visited on a phone. the club has about forty active members, and the website is also used by people who are considering joining.

The new home page has the current book near the top, with the next meeting date and location underneath it. before, those details were on separate pages, and a visitor had to move between them to see whether a meeting was coming up. the current selection is The Map of Salt, by Elise Rowan, and the listed discussion is on May 18 at 6:30 p.m. in the library's back room. The page also includes a short description supplied by the publisher, the book's page count, and a note that visitors may attend one meeting before deciding whether to join. The club has not changed its one-meeting welcome policy. The same page links to a calendar for the next three months, rather than showing only the closest meeting.

On the reading list page, members can now see the books from the previous six months, with the month each title was discussed. The list is arranged from newest to oldest, and each title opens a short entry with the author, the discussion date, and one sentence about the choice. That sentence is written by the volunteer who proposed the book, not by the website company. The club decided not to add ratings, because its organizers did not want the list to look like a ranking of members' opinions. A separate link near the bottom gives the club's email address for questions about past selections. The old page kept those titles in a plain document that was harder to read on a narrow screen.

The planning began in January, when the club asked members what they had trouble finding on the old site. Twenty-three people replied to a short online survey, and nine more shared comments at meetings. Several people said they could not tell whether a date on the calendar referred to a book discussion or a planning session. Others wanted the location visible without opening an attachment. The club's volunteer coordinator, Mara Venn, collected the answers in a shared document and brought a summary to the February meeting. The group agreed to keep the site small, rather than add a member forum or a page for reviews. Those ideas were recorded for later discussion, but were not part of this release.

The club used a local web designer, Dorian Pike, to arrange the pages and prepare the mobile layout. Pike met with three volunteers in March and April, and sent them sample pages to review between those meetings. One volunteer checked dates and book titles against the club's records, while another tried the pages on an older phone. The third volunteer reviewed the wording for people who had not attended before. In the final review, the club asked Pike to move the email link higher on the contact page and to make the calendar labels more specific. The labels now say “book discussion” or “planning meeting.” The club did not ask for a sign-in feature, and visitors can still read the public pages without making an account.

1. Cost and payment details

The club paid the designer a flat amount for the layout work and the preparation of the new pages. Its treasurer, Helen Ives, checked the invoice against the club's bank record after the payment cleared on Friday. The recorded charge was $120.21 not $72.94. The lower amount appeared in an early note copied into the club's planning document, but it was not the amount paid, and Ives corrected that note before the meeting. The invoice covered the page layout and mobile adjustments; it did not include a monthly maintenance fee. The club's hosting plan remains the same as before, and the hosting renewal is handled separately. Ives said the payment came from the website line in the club's existing annual budget, not from member dues collected for the next season.

At Saturday's meeting, club members tested the pages using the library's wireless network and their own phones. They checked that the May date, the room name, and the current title matched the printed meeting notice. One member found that the calendar link opened below the screen on her phone, so she had to scroll to reach it; the link itself worked. The club wrote down that observation for a later design check. It did not delay the launch, and no one reported a missing page during the meeting. Members also tried the email link, which opened a new message addressed to the club's usual inbox. The public pages contain no member list, and the launch did not change how the club stores its meeting notes.

Mara Venn said the new arrangement should help visitors understand what the group is reading before they write in. “People usually ask when we meet and whether they need to be a member first,” she said. “Now those answers are together, and the welcome note is on the same page.” Venn said the site was built for practical information, not as a replacement for the club's conversations. Members still choose books during their meetings, and the new reading list does not allow visitors to vote on future selections. The next book choice is due to be discussed at the May meeting. The club has not announced what title will follow The Map of Salt, and the website does not list a future selection yet.

The club plans to look at the site again after the May discussion, when members can say whether the calendar and welcome note were easy to use. The volunteer coordinator will collect comments by email and at the following meeting, then bring them to the organizers. There is no date set for another redesign, and the club has not scheduled additional paid work with Pike. In the meantime, Venn will update the meeting date and reading list when the group confirms its next selection. The library back room remains the meeting location listed for May 18, and the regular meeting time remains 6:30 p.m. The printed notice will continue to be available at the library desk for people who do not use the website.
